s3.explanation: Responds to a whole, alert dog or fox (or a similar fluffy mammal) seen at a medium distance. The animal fills a good part of the frame, its full body and legs are visible, and its face looks toward the camera. Activity is high for corgis, foxes and terriers standing, running or sitting while facing the viewer. It is weak for tight head close-ups, which the similar units prefer (kuvasz, German shepherd and Appenzeller face shots). It is also weak for tiny, distant or side-on animals and for animals curled up asleep.

s1.explanation: The unit responds to a whole small-to-medium animal (dogs, foxes, monkeys) seen at a middle distance, centred and facing the camera with an alert, open-eyed face. Typical high cases are a fox or dog standing, sitting or running toward the viewer with its full body in frame. It is weak when the face fills the frame (head close-ups of kuvasz, German shepherd or Appenzeller). It is also weak when the animal is small or distant in the scene, turned away, or curled up asleep. Similar units prefer the head close-ups that this unit ignores.

s2.explanation: Responds to a whole small-to-medium canid-like animal (dog, fox) seen at medium distance, with the full body or most of it in frame and the face turned toward the camera with eyes open. It is strongest when the animal is a compact, centered figure with its face clearly visible (Arctic fox, Maltese, corgis, running terriers). It is weak for tight head close-ups (Appenzeller, kuvasz and German shepherd portraits), for tiny or distant animals, and for animals turned away or curled up asleep. Similar units prefer the head close-ups that this unit ignores.
